facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: About 64 feet deep, it is India's largest and deepest stepwells with 13 floors and was built in the 9th century for water harvesting.
facts.text: The stepwell descends through 13 subterranean storeys down into the groundwater reservoir in an inverted pyramidal layout.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: It extends approximately 30 m (100 ft) into the ground, making it one of the deepest and largest stepwells in India.
facts.text: The structure extends approximately 30 metres into the ground, ranking it among the deepest historical stepwells in India.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: It was built by King Chanda of the Nikumbha Dynasty in 9th century AD.
facts.text: Stylistic analyses date the earliest step constructions of Chand Baori to approximately 800 CE during the early medieval era.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Chand Baori, Abhaneri, Dist. Dausa is listed among Centrally Protected Monuments under the Archaeological Survey of India.
facts.text: Chand Baori in Abhaneri is administrated and conserved as a centrally protected monument of national importance by the Archaeological Survey of India.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: However, no epigraphic evidence has been found regarding the construction of the Chand Baori or the adjoining Harshat Mata Temple.
facts.text: While local tradition and state tourism records credit King Chanda of the Nikumbha dynasty with founding the well, epigraphists and historians dispute this attribution because no dedicatory inscription exists at the site, with scholars alternately attributing its construction to the Gurjara-Pratihara or Chahamana dynasties.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: According to Morna Livingston in Steps to Water: The Ancient Stepwells of India, Chand Baori is one of the few stepwells that has 'two classical periods of water building in a single setting'.
facts.text: While popular descriptions claim the monument in its entirety is 1,200 years old, architectural historians dispute this single-period age, showing that while the lower stepped pond dates from the 8th or 9th century, the upper multistoried pavilions and arcades were extensively rebuilt during later Chauhan and 18th-century Mughal periods.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: At the bottom of the well, the air remains 5-6 degrees cooler than at the surface, and Chand Baori was used as a community gathering place for locals during periods of intense heat.
facts.text: Microclimate readings show that ambient air at the bottom of the stepwell stays roughly 5 to 6 degrees cooler than at surface level, serving as a cool public retreat during arid desert heat.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Its lesson — that depth, shade and evaporation can cool a space with no energy at all — is exactly what today's passive-cooling and sunken-courtyard architecture is relearning for a warming climate.
facts.text: Architectural studies demonstrate that the subterranean cooling effect is produced naturally through the high thermal mass of surrounding rock, self-shading stepped geometric walls, and evaporative cooling from the open water body.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The analysis of its architectural and sculptural style suggests it was built in the early 9th century, shortly after the adjoining Chand Baori stepwell was constructed.
facts.text: The Archaeological Survey of India dates the oldest levels of Chand Baori by stylistic comparison with the adjoining ruined Harshat Mata Temple, which was erected in the early 9th century.

sheet.summary: According to local folklore, Chand Baori was conjured overnight in a single night by supernatural spirits who carved an inescapable geometric maze of steps. Archaeological surveys confirm that the site is an engineered subterranean stepwell descending 13 storeys and roughly 30 metres into the ground, utilizing approximately 3,500 stone steps along three walls to harvest rainwater and sustain a natural passive cooling system. Historians disagree over whether the well was founded by a local Nikumbha chieftain named Raja Chanda or commissioned by imperial Gurjara-Pratihara rulers, while also debating how much of the upper pavilion was added during later 18th-century modifications. Because no foundation inscription or dedicatory charter has ever been found, the stepwell's precise founding date, the names of its master architects, and the exact hydrological techniques used to calibrate its microclimate remain unknown.
